speechtext: I am sure my right hon. friend would like me to have the facts correctly stated. As he has just said, his instructions were to leave the resolution at my office.
To be delivered to you.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As the right hon. member knows, I have an office in the House of Commons and one also in the departmental block, where I am obliged to be when dealing with business that appertains to the affairs of the Government. The leader of the Opposition knows that Council meets between two and three o'clock, and at that hour my place of business is in the East Block. The copy which my right hon. friend sent was taken to my office here, which I did not reach until three o'clock. My secretary sent it to me during the course of the debate with a message that it was found on the table, but evidently not delivered to any member of the staff.

I do not dispute the facts as stated by my hon. friend; I merely state that my instructions were to deliver the resolution to him. It was taken to his office here, and I only add that when similar notices were given me while I was Prime Minister they were delivered also to my office in this building, inasmuch as they had reference to House of Commons matters. Hereafter such notices will be delivered to the hon. gentleman at his office in the East Block. I am not finding fault with the Prime Minister at all. I want to make it clear that not only had I no intention of being discourteous to him, but I took the natural steps to notify him of the intention to move this resolution.
Now, what is before the House this afternoon is something which, if I am able at all to estimate the importance of matters that come before Parliament for consideration, is not of cursory or secondary, but of primary and first importance for the decision of hon. members. One hon. gentleman describes the debate as a squabble between one side and the other. Well, everything that comes up for debate in Parliament may be so described, but the question to which hon. gentlemen's minds should be addressed is this: What is the proper thing in the interests of Canada to do? What is the proper decision to give regarding the question propounded in the
amendment that has been moved? It is a question of good faith of political parties; it is a question of the good faith of the House. That is what we have to consider. There is no question before us as to whether there should be a further gratuity to the soldiers of the country. If that were the question before Parliament I would vote in the negative. Is my sincerity doubted, or the sincerity of hon. members who sit around me? By whom is the question of sincerity raised? When we were in office were we or were we not frank with the returned soldiers? We told them definitely, once we had gone the extent we thought the country could go in the matter of cash gratuities, that we could go no further, and we took the penalty of certain hostility among them because of that candour. I put the course we pursued before hon. gentlemen to my left and hon. gentlemen in front of me, before both Oppositions, if you may call them such, en face et de cote, and I ask them whether that is evidence of sincerity or not. We are deciding in this debate, by our votes on this question, whether or not parties are to be held to their pledges. If this resolution is defeated, he who votes against it votes that he is not a supporter of the principle that a party in power is bound by the pledges by which it attained that power.
Now, what was the pledge? Let us inquire dispassionately what it was, and let us inquire, as to the value of the Prims Minister's explanation of the effect of his party's commitment in the terms stated in their platform as transcribed into the resolution. It was this:
Resolved that this Convention declares that the adoption of a system of cash grants to the soldiers and dependents of those who have fallen is the most satisfactory and effective means of civil re-establishment-such grants to be in addition to the present gratuity and to any pension for disability resulting from service.
What is the Prime Minister's statement to-day? He says: There is not embedded in that any promise or pledge whatever. Not embedded there any promise to the five hundred thousand returned men that the Liberal party was committed to give them a further cash grant in addition to the then existing gratuity and pension! Well, all I want to say is this: that if what the hon. leader of the Government says is the only effect of this resolution, then the Liberal party stands under an indictment greater than that levelled against them in the resolution now before

Soldiers' Bonus
the House. Could any returned soldier in receipt of his gratuity and of his pension, having fought, as large numbers of them did, if not the majority, for a further recognition in cash, in the form of a general addition to the grant, could any returned soldier reading that, not come to the conclusion that the Liberal party favoured that for which he had fought? Can the hon. gentleman conceive that any one would come to any other conclusion? "Resolved that this convention declares that the adoption of a system of cash grants to the soldiers and dependents of those who have fallen is the most satisfactory and effective means of civil re-establishment- such grants to be in addition to the present gratuity and to any pension for disability resulting from service." Would not any returned soldier reading this at once think that the Liberal party is in favour of cash grants in addition to the present gratuity? Could any scheme to deceive and mislead the soldiers be more plainly devised than that resolution, if it means what the hon. gentleman says? If it falls short of a promise to the men of a cash grant in ease the party passing that resolution is returned to power, then the indictment of deceit is as bad at [DOT] least as the indictment of repudiation.
That is the resolution. " Oh," says the Prime Minister, " I went through the campaign and I did not promise any cash grants at all." Indeed, Colonel Thompson, who was with him, though he is reported to have made such a promise, actually said he was not in favour of cash grants. He said precisely opposite to what he is reported to have said. Well, are we concerned with Colonel Thompson? Was Colonel Thompson empowered to amend the resolutions of the Liberal party in convention assembled? I doubt, in fact I would question, were I a follower, the right of even the leader of a party to amend those resolutions, to take in his pocket the commission of his party and at his will alter it, whatever the circumstances might be. Colonel Thompson had no such right.
But the leader of the Government says, " I made no promise; I never stood on any platform and promised cash grants." Why, he did not need to do so. He had an official proclamation issued by a committee of which he was the chairman, more than a month before the campaign was launched, and he had commissioned every speaker for the Liberal party to make that promise

under his authority. So he could well afford to be silent while he placed in the hands of every speaker who stood on the platform in his support a document with his photograph on the outside, issued by a committee of which he is declared to be the chairman, that declaration appearing on the frontispiece. That document contains this statement:
That the platform as adopted and quoted below expresses the idea of the great body of delegates of the aims of the Liberal party.
And in that document he quotes the fol lowing, just as it is set out in the resolution before the Chair:
Resolved that this Convention declares, that the adoption of a system of cash grants to the soldiers and dependents of those who have fallen is the most satisfactory and effective means of civil re-establishment-such grants to be in addition to the present gratuity and to any pension for disability resulting from service.
With that in the pocket of every candidate, with that authority to go and repeat the promise embedded in that resolution, what would be the need of the Prime Minister and leader of the party to refer to the subject at all? Nay, more, on platform after platform, men -commissioned by himself, commissioned in writing to say sb, proclaimed this to he the policy of the party, to be its promise and its pledge. And in -my hands now I hold the proclamations, as quoted yesterday, that those candidates issued to the returned soldiers among their electorate promising that this was going to be done. I wonder if even the hon. member for the city of Ottawa, right in the -city where we stand now, will say that he did not utilize that -plank of the Liberal party? Yea, he utilized that platform in this city in association with the Prime Minister himself, and sought to obtain votes on the strength of the pledge contained in the document which I hold in my hand.
That is the condition of affairs that existed in the last campaign. It is not the conduct of elections that we are concerned with. The hon. Prime Minister says, "Oh, you did not do everything that was right." The Government in office in the last Parliament-and I appeal to the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) to say if what I speak is right or not-that Government in office, whether it was politically advantageous or whether it was. not, set about to implement by legislation, and did one by one implement by legislation the pledges that it made to the people before being returned to office. Did any member

Soldiers' Bonus
of the late government stand in his place and say, "Oh, those resolutions were very good in the months of September and October, 1917, but now we are in power, and they don't apply once you get in power if it is two months later." Did any one hear that position taken? No. We set about the fulfilment of our promises, and we took the consequences of that fulfilment-and I want to say that those consequences were not always advantageous to us, and no one knows that better than the 'leader of the Progressive party. One lby one we put those pledges into effect, one by one we fulfilled the contract which we made with the people-a contract which the people accepted when they put us in power, and expected us to carry out.
We were told yesterday: "Oh, the Great War Veterans at their last convention opposed the granting of cash bonuses. I do not know what could be advanced more false, more shadowy, more tricky than the argument that the policy of a great party is subject to alteration by the resolution of some organization in the country. But as a matter of fact there was no such resolution passed by the Great War Veterans. In 1920 they passed a resolution after the convention of 1919, to which I have referred, in which they affirmed themselves definitely in favour of cash grants and pledged themselves to secure such grants if they could. In the face of the position taken by the Great War Veterans the Government of the day declined their request, and said to them: We believe we have gone as far in the general cash grants as is in the interests of the country, and we think that anything further should be in the way of enabling the soldier to help himself through re-training, seeking out various ways in which specially disabled men may be helped in the struggle for life to overcome to some extent the handicaps they labor under as the result of their war service. That was the answer we made to those men. We took the responsibility and the discredit for the straight denial of that request. In the 1921 meeting no resolution was passed changing the position taken by the Great War Veterans in 1920. They passed a general resolution with regard to re-establishment, but took no special position one way or the other on the matter of cash grants. I examined their records in order to make certain of that. But I feel like apologizing, Mr. Speaker, for referring to the action of any association, however respected, however honourable, however worthy of deference its opinion
may be; because I never knew a political party to be in a position of such desperation that it had to seek a loophole of escape from its own solemn pledges, from its own declared policy, by pleading the action and the opinion of some association other than that political party itself. Does the Great War Veterans' Association sit in appeal over Liberal policy? Are they a court of appeal empowered to amend, modify, strike out or enlarge any part of the Liberal platform? Well, possibly they could improve on it; I do not doubt they could. But I would not want to be the leader of the party that submitted to the jurisdiction of any court of appeal in relation to the policy that it puts before the people, save alone the court of appeal of the people themselves. The people accepted the pledge of the Liberal party, accepted the pledge of the Prime Minister, made two years and a half before the election, reaffirmed more than once in the meantime, and reaffirmed last of all in the most solemn way in the handbook of his party which he placed, in the hands of all his speakers throughout the length and breadth of Canada with the authorization to make those . pledges, to state those intimations, to declare that policy. That is the position the hon. gentleman is in to-day.
Now, is it a matter of no concern how we decide this resolution? I do not know that I am particularly concerned as to how others vote than myself. It is a vote of confidence in the Government; I seek no camouflaged position in that regard. If any hon. gentleman wants to say that this Government is to be open and free to repudiate the position it took prior to the contest; to repudiate its solemn pledge and policy and still enjoy the confidence of the House, then it is the right of that hon. gentleman so to vote. If there is anything of more conseqence to that hon. gentleman than the good faith of political pledges, than the good faith of political parties, than the honour of a political party in carrying out its solemn pledge, then the hon. gentleman is the judge of what is more important to him. But if this House is now to give a verdict of acquittal; if this House is now to declare that the platform of 1919 is a "scrap of paper," that it may be accepted as already annulled, abandoned and forgotten, then the consequences of that position must be faced. That platform contains other principles; it contains other policies than those we are discussing to-day. No matter what course the Government takes on any subject em-
Soldiers' Bonus

bodied in that document, on any subject referred to by them in this House through session after session, since and during the campaign, they can never take a position of more direct and defiant repudiation than they took yesterday in relation to this subject. If they are to be acquitted for so doing, then the hon. member of this House who seeks to hold them to their pledges, who seeks to hold them to their avowed policies, will already have cut the ground from under his feet, because he has acquitted them of the very same charge of which he seeks later to hold them guilty. I, for one, will not put myself in that position. I purpose to hold them to their whole chapter of pledges. I purpose to make solid my ground by my vote upon this resolution and through it to declare that I have not lost faith in the political honour of our country. I purpose by my vote here to say-
Oh, oh.

"Oh, oh," say hon. gentlemen; I presume those are the hon. gentlemen who have lost faith, and they have good reason for doing so. I have a recollection of sitting through four sessions of this House when hon. gentlemen who now say "oh" were sitting opposite to me. Though they opposed us in many matters of policy; though they made very many charges against us, they sat through four sessions and never once declared that we had failed in fidelity to the pledges we made by which we obtained office.

Will the right hon. gentleman permit me a correction? Does he not remember when we criticized his government for having repealed Orders in Council passed during the election of 1917 exempting farmers' sons from the application of the law? The repeal of those Orders in Council right after the election we interpreted as lack of good faith toward the farmers' sons.

The Government in office, in the spring of 1918, at a time when the war was at its worst, repealed Orders in Council-or, rather, enacted Orders in Council,-which took away the exemption of farmers' sons between the ages of twenty and twenty-three. That is quite true.
After the election.
Certainly, after the election.

Not before?
[Mr. Meighon.J

No, the Orders in
Council were not in effect then. We removed these exemptions by special Orders in Council, and we did it in obedience to the pledges we made to the people of this country in pursuance of the fact that the throwing of the whole force of the country behind the war effort was the first mandate of the government.
Will the right hon. gentleman allow me to make this correction? The Order in Council exempting the farmers' sons was enacted right before the election and repealed right after.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: If my right hon. friend will allow me, I do not believe I made such a statement. May I repeat what I said yesterday?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I said that the veterans' organizations in Canada had declared themselves opposed to a cash bonus. That is the statement I made to the House.

I will read what the hon. gentleman said. After having declared that the veterans were opposed to the bonus, which by the way the veterans have never declared-I have their resolution here-my hon. friend said:
If my hon. friend wants to Know what my attitude would be on the subject, it could not be
Soldiers' Bonus

any different from the one taken by the returned men themselves, and that is not to grant the cash bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Exactly.
Well, what did I say? I stated that the hon. gentleman had stated his attitude to be-and I assume he spoke for the Government-not to grant any more cash bonuses.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The difference between the right hon. gentleman and myself is that he wants to impose his own will, whereas I want to respect the will of the Veterans.

I will leave the hon. gentleman's retort to answer itself. The point he rose to interrupt me upon was that I had misinterpreted his words. I have read his words, and they are precisely what I said. He announced as Minister of Soldiers' Civil ^Re-establishment his opposition to further cash grants, and the Prime Minister in his statement did the same thing. If, however, in the face of this debate, if in view of the position they are in to-day, the Government wants to lecant or modify its position, there should be ample opportunity to do so. If they are taking the stand, no further cash grants, let them say so. If they want to change from their attitude of yesterday, let them make the change. If they do not intend to change, if they are against further cash grants, then why by interruptions lead any hon. gentleman to any doubt upon the question. They stated yesterday they were opposed to further cash grants. There can be no doubt at all about that. Those are the words of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, who.presides over the department affected. Those are the words reiterated by the Prime Minister himself, and even in to-day's debate is there any hon. gentleman who would not take it, after the Prime Minister's speech, that his Government had definitely decided against further cash grants to soldiers as intimated in the resolution of the Convention of 1919? No. Of the repudiation there is no doubt. Of the making of the pledge there is no doubt. Of its reiteration there is no doubt. Of the authority of the Prime Minister for both the making and the reiteration there is no doubt. Of the repudiation we have had confirmation by one after the other in the debate yesterday. Now, is this Parliament to decide that the making of the pledge followed by its repudiation-the first step in relation to their platform since they came into power- is to go without the rebuke of this Parliament? Shall this House by its vote declare 
that that sort of conduct meets with its approval? This resolution is an opportunity for hon. gentlemen to say that it does not, and I shall vigorously support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker: down in my old home town some years ago a worthy aider-man won undying fame by a single sentence. He had been present at a discussion occupying considerable time, at which speeches had been made very much like the one to which we have just listened by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), and at last he said, "Mr. Chairman, I move that we quit nonsense and proceed to business." We have business to do in this Parliament, hut my right hon. friend and his supporters seem to think that some good end will be served by interrupting business with the motion that has been made to-day, and I pay it a very excellent compliment when I speak of it as nothing worse than nonsense. Does my right hon. friend think any good purpose is to be served by constantly reviving the campaign issues? Does he think he can stand examination on these tests himself?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I venture to say that if any one takes anything like the pains he has taken to look over the work and the speeches preceding the election, he will find cases where my right hon. friend has made statements which have not been followed by results.
I invite the hon. gentleman to pursue the inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend makes a serious denial. I will remind him of an incident in this House that most people will remember. The right hon. gentleman gave what was equivalent to a pledge that there would be no dissolution of Parliament until there had been a redistribution.
I invite the hon. gentleman to quote my words, and he will find that he is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not expect this "nonsense," and, therefore, I have not the quotation, but if this debate goes on, or perhaps a similar debate, I will produce the passage, and I will show what the hon. gentleman said in this House, at the opening of last session, during the debate on the Address, when he was asked to dissolve the

Soldiers' Bonus
House, and when it was argued that the government did not represent the people. The Montreal Gazette at that time endorsed the position of the right hon. gentleman and declared that it would he an outrage to dissolve Parliament until the West had obtained its representation. The hon. gentleman told us very truly that the West was going to be entitled to so many more members, and he said "If we were to dissolve the House on any issue in advance of that time we would be doing a great injustice to the western provinces." He has done that injustice. He has perpetrated what the Montreal Gazette declared would be an outrage by the dissolution of Parliament. We are going to have a period now of five years during which the western provinces are going to be denied proper representation. My hon. friend has asked for an instance, and I give it to him now. With further investigation, we might give him other instances. Soon after my right hon. friend became Prime Minister he went out west and in Calgary made his declaration in regard to the tariff policy, saying that the country had a right to know what tariff they were going to have, and declaring that before Parliament was dissolved they would have before them a tariff revision in black and white.
Better get the speech and quote it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman deny it?
He is not correctly quoting what I said.
It was in the Speech from the Throne.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Speech from the Throne promised tariff revision. So far as that is concerned, the hon. gentleman monkeyed with the tariff question for years. They had Sir Thomas White telling the House that the tariff revision was overdue and that it ought to come that year, but it did not come, and then another year passed, and it did not come. Then they had the Tariff Commission which wandered all over the country. They made a solemn declaration in the Speech from the Throne that during that session they would bring down tariff revision. Is that statement true, or do I invent it?

If the hon gentleman invites an answer, I will give it. The words he quotes were not used. What was stated was that a tariff revision would
be brought down in due course. The interposition of the American situation on the tariff question was good and sufficient reason for postponing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman not only put in the Speech from the Throne that statement, but instructed the then member for Prince Edward Island, Mr. Mclsaac, in moving the address, to declare that the tariff revision was imperative. It was said, "Now is the day of tariff revision." Was that true? With that promise in the Speech from the Throne they let the session go by, and dissolved Parliament without a tariff revision at all. What right has the right hon. gentleman to talk of the honour of Parliament in the way he does, after these two instances I have given? My hon. friend did these two things, and I have no doubt if we would make an investigation we would find many more. Again I say, he cannot afford to challenge discussion along these lines. The question whether that resolution with regard to the soldiers' bonus at the convention of 1919 was or was not a wise one,
I am not going to discuss, but this I do say, that it was not an issue in the recent election. If it were correct that it was an issue affecting the elections recently held, there would be some ground for the hon. gentleman's complaint, but we all know that, whatever may have been said at that convention, at the time the election came on that question had ceased to be an issue in this country. I had the pleasure of taking some part in the election. I spoke at a number of meetings. I never mentioned the soldiers' bonus, and never heard it mentioned. My opponent never mentioned it. It never was an issue at all. So that I say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no reason in the world why that should be treated as an issue affecting the election.
My right hon. friend talks of the appeals to the people on which we won the election. He cannot talk on any appeal on which be won his election. Whenever he appealed he was met from ocean to ocean, to a degree tnat was never experienced before in the history of Canada, by a repudiation of his Government. The soldiers' bonus was not an issue in the election, so far as any knowledge of mine goes. I never spoke of it, and my opponent never spoke of it. I spoke at many meetings in many parts of the country, I never heard it mentioned. I was never asked a question about it. It may have been an issue in former times. The country accepted the judgment of the

Soldiers' Bonus
committee of the House, presided over by that excellent member, Mr. Cronyn, as a settlement of the soldier bonus question. Before that committee the door was opened to consider any matters that might arise in connection with soldiers. But when he says that was an issue at the last election, and that on that issue we came back to power, I tell my hon. friend he is entirely mistaken.

I do not propose to detain the House for any length of time in a discussion of this matter which has been pretty vigorously threshed out by my hon. friends on both sides of the House. The crux of the amendment moved by my right hon. friend is that it levels the charge of insincerity and of disregard to the niceties of political honour against the Government and my hon. friends who sit opposite. That is a very serious accusation to level, and if I were convinced that it had substantial foundation. I would have no hesitation in supporting the amendment of my right hon. friend. But, Mr. Speaker, I am not so convinced, and I will very briefly give the House my reasons. I do not now propose to enter into any discussion as to whether the resolution dealing with this matter passed at the Liberal convention, 1919, was passed in good faith or not. I have no reason to believe that it was passed other than in good faith, and for the reason that every one in this House and out of it knows that at that particular moment, in the midsummer of 1919, our soldiers were being demobilized, they were being returned from Europe and there was a feeling throughout the whole Dominion, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that everything we could do for the returned men who fought so gloriously overseas was only what Canada should do for them. That was the atmosphere at that time. But if I say to the Government, " Because you had a resolution approving the principle of a soldiers' bonus at your convention in 1919, you must disregard all that has taken place since then and implement that resolution," then I am going a little too far. That is the position I take in this connection, and let me very briefly state my reasons. The Liberal party then in Opposition in this House might be, and probably were, perfectly consistent at that time. But if public opinion throughout Canada has changed upon that question in the last three years since June, 1919, and if other things have intervened, then, in

my judgment, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and my hon. friends opposite are not acting dishonourably in stating that the time has passed for the giving of a bonus to the returned soldiers. That is the position I take.
What are the reasons? We have our financial situation for one thing. I speak so much about it, I am afraid I make myself wearisome sometimes upon the point; but I think anyone who studies the financial position of Canada is aware that it is one of the gravest things facing this country. We know that the finances of Canada will not, at the present time, stand a vast contribution by way of a soldier's bonus. We recognize that fact; we recognize also the fact that three years ago a definite policy was followed by the government of the day, in my judgment a wise policy, a policy endorsed by Parliament at that time, for giving assistance to returned soldiers, and already a sum amounting to almost a hundred million dollars has been spent in the soldiers' land settlement scheme. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) brought in the soldiers' land settlement scheme; I supported him at that time, and I think yet that, while th6 scheme may have had defects in its operation, it was soundly conceived. I am quite willing to admit that my right hon. friend, and the then government of which he was the head, endeavoured to administer that scheme in the best interest of the returned soldiers of this country. For these considerations, I cannot agree with my right hon. friend and the mover and the seconder of this resolution, that because the present Government, in view of changed circumstances, cannot come forward and provide a cash bonus for the soldiers, it is acting in bad faith or dishonestly. I am anxious, as I am sure all other hon. members are, that good faith in matters of public policy should be observed. I must, however, confess that 1 am afraid there is possibly a little bit more behind the moving of this amendment than the mere vindication of political honour in this House, and I am led to that conclusion by a statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who spoke to the resolution. In that statement, my hon. friend said to the Government: "You should either implement the plank in your platform, or state that you took an unfair advantage of us in the election." That is placing the reasons for a consideration of this question upon altogether too low a level

Soldiers' Bonus
and, consequently, I cannot agree with my right hon. friend and his supporters in the amendment which they have moved. The amendment, as the leader of the Opposition has stated, is a direct vote of confidence in the Government-
Want of confidence.

Yes, I would scarcely expect my right hon. friend to move a motion of confidence in the Government. It is a direct motion of want of confidence in the Government. What does that mean if we look at the situation fairly? If we carry the thing to its logical conclusion, it means that if this motion carries, this Government is out and we shall have another election. I do not think my hon. friends to my right for a moment expected or desired that this would be carried to that conclusion, and for that reason I shall oppose the amendment of the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs.)
A good deal has been said in the debate about the conduct of the election. I trust that in this House we shall soon get away from an examination of what happened prior to December 6. I could tell you, Mr. Speaker, in all confidence, and I will state it here for the full information of the House, that if I and my hon. friends around me desired to pursue that line, we could bring a very emphatic indictment against not only my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), but some of my hon. friends on the other side of the House. Possibly in the course of the election I may have said something; for in the heat of elections, we sometimes get beyond the bounds of political proprieties or what should.be the political proprieties. But I cannot see that much good will come to this House from continuing these discussions.
As I have already stated, this Parliament has very serious business to do. Let us get down to the consideration of that business. When my hon. friends opposite are not pursuing a course that I conceive to be in the best interest of the country, then I stand here to tell them so, and to oppose them in that course. That is the angle from which I approach my duties in this House; and because the amendment moved by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) approaches it from another angle, I cannot support him, and I shall oppose it.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate started this afternoon, I had no intention of taking part in it, and I would not do so now but for the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) brought in a statement which I made yesterday evening regarding what Colonel Thompson h'ad said at Port Arthur. I was not, of course, present at the meeting of the Prime Minister; I think I was out in some section of my constituency or somebody else's at that time. But at any rate Colonel Thompson is quoted exactly as I quoted him yesterday evening, and I did the courtesy to the Prime Minister of sending him the paper in which the quotation was given. I might point out that this paper is not a political paper; it takes an absolutely independent stand. It did not support me in the election, so that I am quoting from a paper which is not a supporter of mine. If I wished to go on quoting-and I shall not take up any time in quoting anything- I could give a quotation from a speech of my hon. friend which might embarrass him severely in this House. As is reported in the Port Arthur press, he took the stand in that city that the government of Mr. Meighen at that time was committing the unpardonable crime of appointing its friends to the Senate. That was one of the statements quoted in connection with his speech, but I do not wish to deal with that. The hon. gentleman who leads the Government stated, in the speech which he made this afternoon, that this pledge of the Liberal party was wiped out because of the actions of the Great War Veterans Then I ask, as has been asked before: Why do they include it in their platform in October, 1921? Their platform was sent out at the beginning of the election, and it would have been the easiest thing in the world to delete that part of it since my hon. friend says now that they had no intention of carrying it out. As a matter of fact, I hold in my hand what has been handed to me by an hon. member from Vancouver, namely, a statement put out in the press by three Liberals who ran for Vancouver, absolutely pledging themselves to a cash gratuity. There is no doubt they based that pledge on the platform of the Liberal party. The Prime Minister also said that in 1919-I think I am quoting him correctly; I hope he will correct me if I am not-when that resolution was passed at the convention, they favoured cash grants, but they have changed their opinion since. We were giving cash grants at that time to soldiers returning from overseas. Every soldier, who served over-
Soldiers' Bonus

seas and who returned, received from the government that was in power at that time, a cash grant running anywhere, I think, from three hundred to six hundred dollars. So that we were giving cash grants; and unless that resolution meant a further cash grant it could mean nothing at all. I presume now that it might well be said to have meant nothing. My hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), I think, said that this was a camouflage motion, and that it really was not intended to get a bonus for the soldiers. I admit that very frankly. The party in this corner of the House, which were in power from 1917 to 1921, again and again refused to consider cash grants for soldiers. I made myself unpopular amongst some of the returned men by openly declaring my opposition to the principle. This resolution has nothing to do with any request for a grant, and so far as I am personally concerned I do not believe that the thing is possible. I think it is a financial impossibility to give $2,000 to each of the returned men. The only thing the resolution does is to condemn the putting into a platform, for political purposes, of a promise which the party that makes it has no intention of carrying out. The resolution condemns such unscrupulous tactics; it declares that pledges which are not intended to be implemented should not be exploited for election purposes. In other words, it is a condemnation of the breaking of faith with the people of the country after a party has been elected on a pledge which it has used during an election campaign. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is quoted as having said at one time, in a jocular way, that platforms were made to get in on but not to stand on, and it seems that that piece of pleasantry has become an established political principle. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said a moment ago that he did not favour the resolution because it sought something that was not possible. Let me repeat once more that the resolution does not demand that the Government should give a cash bonus to the soldiers. It is a resolution condemning the principle, or rather the lack of principle, of advocating platforms in the country before election and refusing to carry them out afterwards. Now, my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has been accused of having broken his pledges. Let me say that I got elected on a platform put forward by Sir Robert Borden in 1917, and that we carried out every one of the twelve planks of which it was composed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Including Sir Robert
Borden.

Sir Robert Borden carried himself out, because he happened to be so unfortunate as to fall ill; and I would say in regard to the laughter which I hear on the other side that I have yet to see in this House, on either side, a man for whom I have greater respect than I have for Sir Robert Borden. I saw him in this House during the better part of four years, and I have-and I believe my hon. friends on the other side have-the highest respect for the attitude which that right hon. gentleman took on all questions. I have said it in private, and I say .it in public now, since the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) has seen fit to interject the remark he has made, and his friends sneeringly approve it, that I have never seen Sir Robert Borden in the House of Commons, on any question that was discussed, taking what I considered to be a narrow or bigoted stand; and I think that is a tribute which can be paid with pride to any man who has sat in Parliament as long as the right hon. Sir Robert Borden did.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) dismisses this resolution as so much nonsense. He points out that my right hon. leader promised that there should be redistribution before an election and that he did not carry out that promise. Well, the Minister of Finance and his colleagues are in power now, and I do not notice any remarks about redistribution in the Speech from the Throne this year, although they have an opportunity of doing what they think we should have done. It has also been said that the bonus question was not an issue in the election. I grant that in many cases it was not; but it was made an issue by the platform of the Liberal party, and it was used by those members I have quoted and by some of the supporters of the men whom I opposed on public platforms. It was made an issue by the party-opposite in various parts of the Dominion during the election and was used as a means of securing the soldier's vote. If the present Government had wished to be fair in regard to this question they would have deleted the pledge from their platform when they put that platform before the people. Now, Sir, I do not wish to take up more time.
Hear, hear.

Let us get down to business.

Soldiers' Bonus

My last remark seems
to please some hon. gentlemen. Well, I am glad to be able to please them to that extent at any rate, although some of them during the last four years were not so very considerate of the time of the House or so anxious to help expedite matters. Let me point out again that the resolution does not advocate a bonus for soldiers, but condemns the making of promises by political parties who afterwards refuse to carry them out. I do not believe in that type of political warfare and I shall vote for the resolution.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. SEXSMITH (Lennox and Addington) :
speechtext: I want to ask two questions, Mr. Speaker: Are we to understand from the mover of the resolution that there shall be given a cash grant to the returned soldiers?
No.
Or does the hon. member imply that there has been an absolute refusal to assist the soldiers, and that the Government does not intend to give any further help to them?
No.
Then we have lost three hours and a half.

In view of the wording of the resolution I am somewhat surprised at the question asked by the last speaker (Mr. Sex-smith). The resolution is clear and definite. It is a condemnation of the principle of giving pledges, before an election, which a party has no intention of carrying out. As I listened to the various speeches I could not help thinking of an inscription on the walls of another chamber in this building, "The spirit of the printed word". 1 also recalled an address delivered in this Chamber a year ago in the debate on the address by the present Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King), and I am going to quote a few words from his remarks. What I am about to read was his carefully prepared peroration which he read to this House. He said:
What is it, Mr. Speaker, that works havoc in human lives, that destroys the noblest of friendships, that blights all that is most sacred in our human relations? It is the loss of confidence that comes through disillusionment, through the broken pledges, the shattered ideals, the lost visions, the vanished faith. Cruel, indeed, it is when that breach in confidence comes between man and man, between friend and friend, between race and race, between nation and nation; but when it comes between a people and its Government, there is no saying what injury it may ultimately work.
What we need to-day is to seek to restore to the people faith in our parliamentary institutions, through conceding their right of control over the Parliament of the country. We know that there are rights under the law; that there are powers under the constitution; these we are prepared to concede to the limit. But is there no such thing in our national economy as public morality? Is there nothing binding in conscience and in honour between those who rule a people and those who have permitted them to rule?
There are the words of the present leader of the Government on that occasion, and yet to-day he attaches no importance to the promise that was made a part of his platform, which was re-affirmed, and, as has been pointed out, circulated throughout the Dominion in the handbook of the Liberal party during the election of 1921.
I know that in my constituency twenty-four pamphlets were circulated by the Liberal party, being placed in the mail boxes throughout the rural districts after dark presumably so no one might know who was doing it. And this was one of the pledges made to the people, which the people had a right to believe would be carried out by those who were appealing for their support.
I was a little surprised at the statement' made by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) this afternoon. "Why," he said, "this stuff is all nonsense. We are just wasting time. Why do you pay any attention to things embodied in .platforms, election addresses and promises?" It seems to me that I heard the hon. minister make a similar statement some time ago. He was quite frank and candid. This was before the election. Speaking in this House on May 18, 1920, he said:
Now, responsibility generally sobers men.
Yes, responsibility sobers men, and he is evidently sober now. The hon. gentleman who leads the Government is also evidently sober to-day. I suppose that would imply that they were not sober when these statements were made to the people. What else did he say on that occasion?
I think myself that we will find that we are all prone in framing platforms to put things perhaps a little more strongly than is wise and we all find when we come to the responsibilities of office that we may have to modify our views.
He said we may have to modify our views. I am not going to take up the time of the House in quoting from the Liberal platform, but I do want to call attention to something else. The hon. Minister of Finance has stated that the leader of the official Opposition (Mr. Meighen) did not keep the pledges and promises
Soldiers' Bonus

which he made to the people, and he referred to the revising of the tariff and other matters. What happened in regard to them? Just about a year ago, on February 15, 1921, we find that the present Prime Minister moved a resolution in this House in amendment to the Address in the following words:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers do not possess the confidence of this House or of the country, and that their retention of office constitutes a usurpation of the powers of popular government.
This is all he had to say on the matter: We are not going to discuss tariff, redistribution or anything of that kind; the Government has no right to legislate, and its retention of office is a usurpation of power. The right hon. leader of the Opposition, who was then Prime Minister, went to the people, and he had to deal with the promises and platforms made by the then leader of the Opposition, now Prime Minister of this country, who to-day asks hon. members assembled here, the representatives of the people of Canada, to attach no importance to promises and pledges that were made while his party was in opposition. Has our public life become so degraded that this is the lesson we are to teach the youth of our country? Is this the ideal we are to set in public life-that we are to repudiate promises made to the electors of Canada. I say it is an insult to any hon. member to ask him to disregard the pledges and promises which he made to his electorate.
Now, Sir, this is not a new policy which has been developed by the Liberal party. Eleven days after the armistice was signed, in fact the ink was scarcely dry on the signatures, when an organization meeting of the Liberals of Western Ontario was held in the city of London which was addressed by the leader of the Liberal party of that day (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Reference was made to this matter at that time, and a resolution was passed that our soldiers' claims would be one of the first things that the Liberal party would deal with if returned to power. When I came into the House last night and heard the Prime Minister and the Minister of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Beland) repudiate these promises, stating, "We do not intend to do anything with them," I immediately recalled the statements that were made upon that occasion. I hold in my hand the London Advertiser of November 20th 1918, the official organ of

the Liberal party in Western Ontario, then as it is now. Two things featured the speeches then made. One was referred to by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) relative to promises which had been made to the farmers of Canada regarding exemption from militia service. It was taken up by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on that occasion and he condemned the Government of the day for having violated its promises, and I am going to read from the official organ of the Liberal party exactly what he did say. Here it is:
Delegations of farmers came to Ottawa, thousands of them, to ask the Government to be as good as its word. They were told no, it could not be done, and the reason the Government gave was that the military situation was serious. The military situation at that time, that is about the month of May, was certainly very serious, but sir, are we to believe that the men who introduced that policy, who told us that it was absolutely necessary that we should have this compulsory recruiting, that it should be universal-are we to believe that when they made that promise, are we to suppose that they believed that this war could be fought without reverses? Did not they know last fall that we were to have a last offensive of the German armies in France ; did not they think it was possible that these armies might suffer reverses of their own; and that when they gave that promise they might meet with a situation such as this? If they did, then sir, there is only one of two things, they made the promise to the farmers in ignorance or they made it in bad faith. I know what their motive was.
This matter has been referred to so often in this House that I am afraid hon. members opposite have not followed the course of the war with any degree of care. It is very easy to look backward and see where you have made mistakes and where you might have done better; but when we are subject to censure by hon. members opposite, in view of what has happened and it is on record, I say that it ill becomes any hon. member to your right, Sir, to taunt the Government of that day with having put in force the law which was then enacted. If hon. members will refer to the report of General Allenby, Commander-in-Chief of the Egyptian Expeditionary Forces, to the War Office, issued from his general headquarters on September 18th, 1918, they will find that he states how his army had been depleted by reason of the situation which had developed on the Western Front, and he points out that in the first week of April 1918 the 52nd Division had been withdrawn and hurried to the Western Front, that in tfie second week of that month the 74th Division had also been withdrawn and hurried to the same destination. Those

Soldiers' Bonus
withdrawals were followed by nine yeomanry regiments, five and a half siege batteries, ten British battalions, and five machine gun companies. In May fourteen battalions of British infantry were withdrawn, and he had to fall back until his depleted forces were made up by fresh recruits front India. I mention this to show the desperate situation on the western front at that time, and the need for men to justify the cancellation of exemption from military service at that time. It was not until after troops had been sent him to take the place of those that had been removed to the western front that he achieved the victory which was the deciding factor in bringing the war to an end. Now, this is a matter which has apparently escaped the observation of some hon. gentlemen opposite; yet they readily point to the cancellation of the farmers' exemptions as a justification for the attitude of this Government and of the Liberal party to repudiating one of the pledges contained in their platform.
This resolution has been referred to by a number of speakers in the party to my left as one that should not be taken very seriously. It struck me that they were very anxious to find some excuse for not supporting a vote of censure upon the Government with regard to its attitude on this question. The one who considers himself the alpha and omega of the Farmers' movement in Ontario, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) says that the discussion has not been very edifying. Well, I do not think that he added very much by the remarks which he himself made. I followed him closely; I believe it is the first time he has spoken in this House. He has written most voluminously in regard to the movement of the Farmers' party in Ontario, but when his constituents and the people of Ontario read Hansard to-morrow I fear they will not be very much edified by his contribution to the debate. Other hon. members to my left have made some observations. But I want to point out that a violation of pledge of this kind recalls to one's mind the justification of the allied countries for taking the action they did in August, 1914-the repudiation of a solemn obligation by Germany, an obligation which they characterized as a "scrap of paper." Many sacrifices were made in that war; millions of lives were laid down for a principle; yet in this Parliament to-day we are
calmly asked by the Prime Minister and his supporters to attach no importance to pre-election promises. Conditions, they say, have changed since they adopted that plank in their platform. But have they overlooked the fact that the policy in question was reaffirmed by them during the recent election campaign with a view to getting the support of the soldier electors? If they knew they were not going to put it into effect, then they deliberately set about to deceive the very men who made such tremendous sacrifices that we might be permitted to assemble here in Parliament this atfernoon.
Mr. JOHN L. BROWN (Lisgar) : The hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Sutherland) has seen fit to criticise the remarks made by those who sit in the Progressive group. I have been brought up to believe that we should be able to give a reason for the faith that is in us, and it is incumbent upon me to be able to give a reason why I shall vote as I intend to do upon this resolution.
I am not very greatly concerned In coming to the defence of the Government in this matter. I am not greatly concerned in what may have been their attitude before the election and how it squares with the position they take now, any more than I am with the attitude taken by the official Opposition, either before the election or at the present time. To what extent this question was an issue in the election I am not prepared to say. I was In a happy and unique position in my constituency: there was no one prepared officially to endorse either the hon. gentlemen now sitting opposite or the then government. Opposed to me was a gentleman who repudiated the Union government and its successor, the National what-do-you-call-it- the big name-and all its works, as well as the right hon. leader of the Opposition. But this question was not an issue In the constituency of Lisgar. As has been pointed out, the only issue raised in that country

and we could not get any discussion of public and really important questions at all -had to do with the question of the United Grain Growers. It is worth noting that in that section of the country, where that particular question was best understood- and we did understand it-the electors spoke in no uncertain terms. Hon. gentlemen on the Government benches will take note of that, just as well as hon. gentlemen of the official Opposition.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argen-teuil, Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The sum of $1,353,922.50 was voted for the fiscal year 1921-22 for salaries of

the permanent staff at Ottawa, and it is estimated that it will require $1,462,770 for the service during the fiscal year 1922-23, an increase of $108,847. As shown in the schedule, the permanent inside service consists of 832 employes, an increase of ten over the fiscal year 1921-22. Statutory increases under the Civil Service Act have been provided for in every instance, and the balance of the increase shown is due to the application of the classification. The increase in the number of employees is accounted for as follows: Number of positions in 1921-22, estimated, were 822, less position of superintendent accountant, deleted. Then there was a transfer from the Commission of Conservation by Order in Council No. 2550, of the 20th of July, 1921, of eight persons. The following employees, namely, economic adviser, hydro-electrical engineer, outside agent, librarian, principal map draughtsman, four senior clerk stenographers, and a messenger clerk, account for the difference between the 822 estimated for and the 832 employed in the department.

I do not know that this explanation quite covers the matter. Take the assistant office engineers, for example. They are fairly highly paid employees and they have increased from 15 to 31, or over 100 per cent. There are undoubtedly reductions in some other instances, but what is the reason for this increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These increases were dated back to April, 1919, and they were not classified until this year.
I am not asking as to the salaries; the minister has given some explanation regarding them. I am speaking as to the number of the office engineers, which has increased from 15 to 31.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are no increases, but there have been changes made by the classification of the Civil Service Commission, and these changes account for the difference.

I have no
doubt my hon. friend has given a good deal of thought to the Estimates. I suppose I am right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I suppose so.

Well, does
he consider that the Estimates as pro-

duced are a proper exemplification of the platform of economy?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As I am informed, this is a matter over which I have no control.

No control
over your employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have been in charge of the department for a short time, but I do not appear to have control over the number of employees, or the classification; my hon. friend appears to have provided for that.

If the hon. minister
thinks or believes that he has no control over the number of his employees, then with all my respect for him personally, I really think he should resign and let some one else take his place who will have control.
Are you looking for it?
When I was head of that department I controlled the number of employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When I liave been in charge for a time I will try to control the employees too.

I am very glad of that promise of improvement, but I do not want the House to get the impression-at least, it will not be my fault if it does-that any minister does not absolutely control the number of officers in his department; that is to say, unless he fails to get the approval of Council, he can reduce the number to any extent he deems advisable, and the responsibility is his; he cannot shift it on to anybody else.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not seeking to evade responsibility for control of the department. I quite understand, even from my short tenure of office, that one has the authority to carry on with a lesser number of civil servants than he may find in his department; but I think my hon. friend will agree with me that it is advisable to be well-informed and to go slowly before starting to make changes. I have said that I think the department is very well organized; I still think so; but perhaps after mature consideration I may find places where more economy may ba exercised.

My	hon.
friend is quite right in connection with the classification. There is no doubt that former temporary emloyees have been
drafted into the service, and very properly so, under the rules of the Civil Service Commission. For example, there is an apparent saving under the heading of Clerical Assistance from $40,000 to $25,000. That saving, as it is taken up, accounts in part for the increase in my hon. friend's vote, because those temporaries are made permanent and therefore added to the list. I am quite well aware of that. But take travelling expenses and sundries; that cannot be blamed on the Civil Service Commission. There is an increase of 30 percent. Why that increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I admit that personally I have not interfered with the services of any one of the departments over which I have control. I think it will be generally agreed that with eight hundred or nine hundred employees, while one is trying to get acquainted with them, there is not very much time to examine very closely as to where certain services might be dispensed with. This again is accounted for by a change. Travelling expenses and sundries, $32,000, shows an increase of $10,000 over 1921-22. It is estimated that $22,000 will be required to meet expenses of the permanent Inside Service officials at Ottawa who may be travelling on Government business, and an amount of $10,000 will be necessary to cover the expenditure connected with telegrams, postage, subscriptions to newspapers, express charges, cab hire, washing towels, and for other small items relating to the Inside Service of the department at Ottawa. The amount estimated for 1921-22 for travelling expenses was $12,000, but, on account of additions to the permanent Inside staff through blanketing-in Orders in Council or Section 79 of the Dominion Lands Act, it will be necessary to increase the item in order to meet the requirements of this service. The expenditure from 1st April, 1921, to 31st December, 1921, was $17,036.78. I am advised that the $10,000 is very largely charged from other services and is drawn by the very same civil servants who may be travelling. Those expenses will now be all taken out of this particular vote. There is therefore no real increase in this vote, it being in the nature of a transfer.
Is the total expense for the past year $17,300?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, the total expense from April 1st, 1921, to December 31, 1921, nine months, was $17,036.78.
Supply-Interior
Then why are you endeavouring to increase the vote for nine months? The old vote would just about cover that.

I notice at the foot of page 78, dealing with senior file clerks, that the number is increased from twelve to twenty-nine. I thought at first that possibly some junior grades were moved up, but looking at the top of page 79 I find that even this year there are twenty-three, or a reduction of only two on the number last year. That would mean seven less in the junior grades, but there is an increase of seventeen in the senior grades. There is one other item on page 79, clerk stenographers, increased from 96 to 111, while the juniors have been reduced by ten. It may be that' these two items together make up 30 per cent or 40 per cent of the entire increase in the department, and that the Civil Service Commission is responsible, although it would hardly seem to me to be so on a cursory inspection. On the other hand, it may be that the pruning knife which was applied to most of the departments by the late government-and which, very naturally, was very much resented- having been dropped, the economies which resulted are now being made up for by a constant expansion. I do not know whether the hon. minister can answer the question off hand. I do not ask to hold up the passing of the vote because of that, but I should like to know, and possibly the House might be interested too, in his explanation before all the Estimates are passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A large proportion of the $10,000 item, practically all of it I am informed, is taken from the vote for other purposes in the interests of which these men were travelling. They are now grouped together, have become civil servants and can no longer procure money from that vote; therefore you find the item of $12,000 added to the travelling expenses for the purpose of covering those items. In answer to the hon. member for St. John, I thought I made it very clear that there is no increase, except to the extent of the eight who joined the service and were transferred from the Conservation Commission staff to that of the Department of the Interior. On the other hand, the items as changed simply represent, so far as my information goes, the changes made by the Civil Service Commission with respect to classification, and that I take it is fixed. I have not attempted

to interfere with it, assuming that the Civil Service Commission have control.
What are the functions and duties of the Publicity Agent for whom $2,400 is provided on page 77? There are two or three other new items in the same group.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that the publicity agent advertises the parks and playgrounds over which the department has control, and takes steps to induce tourists and other interested persons to visit them.

For the encouragement of the minister and to inspire in him hopes for the future, I want to say this: it is difficult in a large department such as the Interior to avoid increases, particularly in the face of the statutory increases of civil servants. This year I find that his increases amount to approximately $108,000. In the year of which I was reminded by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), when I was Minister of the Interior-and I know the previous reductions were the same-notwithstanding the obstacles, notwithstanding that the work of the department very considerably expanded, we took care of all statutory increases and of all the actual work and effected an actual reduction of $6,200.

What is the explanation of the increased amount asked for printing and stationery?	Members of the
House are literally flooded with stationery and printed matter from nearly every department; it seems to me that a good deal of it could be lopped off. It looks like a case where we should have a decrease rather than an increase, particularly in times like these.
Mr. STEWART	(Argenteuil) : The
money is needed to pay for books of various descriptions,-index books; land patent record books, etc., file backs, special paper for patents, printed forms, purchase of typewriters and stationery required for the general use of the Inside Service at Ottawa. There are 250 typewriters constantly in use in the Inside Service, the cost of repairs and supplies in connection with which amount to a very large figure each year. The expenditure under the head of printing and stationery during the past three years has been as follows: fiscal year 1919-20, $58,603.64; 1920-21, $70,367,.16; 1921-22, $77,000. The amount estimated for 1922-23 is $13,000 more than the

Supply-Interior
amount of the estimated expenditure for 1921-22, but as strict economy is being practised it is thought that $58,000 will be sufficient to cover this service.

But still, why the increase? We were using typewriteri before. Prices are going down; paper is a good deal cheaper than it was. I may say that in order to effect a saving, the Department of the Secretary of State went through the old war departments and got hold of all available typewriters, and the departments were asked not to purchase any new ones. Is my hon. friend putting this large increase into the purchase of typewriters?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, I
did not say so. That is simply one of the items.

Then why the
increase?

I was going to ask
the question about printing and stationery which the minister has just answered. We find ourselves at a loss in criticising any of these Estimates, because as soon as we speak about them we find that everything is covered by the reclassification. This reclassification is like charity; it covers a - multitude of sins. Of what avail are our criticisms of these Estimates if every time we ask, why these increases, there is a tendency to hide behind the Civil Service Commission or the reclassification; and because of that we cannot go into the details. I realize that the heads of these departments are new men and cannot be expected to be familiar with all the details. At the same time, they are responsible for their departments, and we want to impress upon them that the country expects of them anci will demand of them, classification or no classification, a reduction of these Estimates commensurate with the reduction in the cost of living and the price of supplies, due regard being had also to the country's diminishing income.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the
general vote of the department as a whole we are able to show a considerable saving. I hope no one would intimate that I have been endeavouring to hide behind the Civil Service Commission in connection with this matter; that was not my thought. So far as Civil Service salaries are concerned I must confess that we appear to have very little control,-I may say frankly, none at all. My hon. friends have pointed out that we have control so far as the reduction
of the service is concerned; that is quite true. I think my predecessor in office was managing the department very well; I have every confidence in his ability to do that. It may be that further savings could be effected, but after some years' experience with civil servants I do not know that you can get along by reducing your staffs all at once. I am not prepared to say at this juncture whether or not further reductions can be made, but I do say that if savings can be made in any quarter, I am determined to make them. This vote is asked largely on the representations of the officials of the department. It is stated that the money is needed; if it is not needed it will not be spent.

There is a new appointment here: Economic Adviser, $4,200. Is this new Economic Adviser appointed to assist in the expenditure of the additional $100,000, or is he to assist the minister in reducing the expenditure? It seems rather a peculiar thing to appoint an economic adviser and then ask for an increase of $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I trust
my hon. friend does not assume that I am thoroughly familiar with the titles of all the different officers in this huge department. I do not pretend to be able to give the information, and I Would not try. This official came over from the Conservation Commission. I do not know why he has this particular title. Indeed, I may say I have sometimes wondered at the multiplicity of titles in the Civil Service.
We voted against titles some time ago in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not seem to have reduced them in the Civil Service.

I was very glad a moment ago to hear the declaration from the minister that he proposed to practise as rigid economy as possible in the administration of his department. I commend that attitude, and trust that it will be fully appreciated and practised by the Government as a whole.
Since yesterday I have taken the trouble of getting a little information in respect to the increasing cost of civil government in this country, and to my mind it is quite alarming in view of the circumstances in which this country finds itself financially. I find, for instance, that in 1903 the total vote for civil government in Canada was
Supply

Interior

in round figures $1,404,000; that is twenty years ago. In 1913, ten years later, it had increased to $5,372,000, and between 1913 and 1923 the cost of civil government has grown to over $11,000,000, or an increase of almost 100 per cent in the last ten years. That, to my mind, is a subject of very serious importance to this House. Parliament votes the money and naturally we are reluctant to cut down the Estimates that a minister asks for. I know that that is the attitude with which I approach the matter myself. I am anxious to see the public services carried on efficiently and effectively, but the time has come, I think, when we must frankly face the situation.
In respect to the department over which my hon. friend has supervision, I find that the increase has been equally great. In 1903 the total expenditure for civil government in the Department of the Interior, including salaries and contingencies was roughly $135,000; that is twenty years ago. In 1913 it had grown to $1,025,000. Now at that time the Department of Immigration was also in the Interior Department. Consequently, the figures I have just given include the expenditure for immigration purposes, as well as the conduct of the business of the Department of the Interior. At the present time the minister is asking for a vote of $1,462,770 for salaries, and $115,000 for contingencies, or a total of $1,577,770 for civil government in this department alone. That is an increase in the last ten years for civil government alone of $575,000 in the Interior Department, and if we include the vote for the Department of Immigration, which amounts to almost $275,000, we find that the cost of administering these services has increased by almost $1,000,000 in the last ten years. This does not take into account the cost of running the department outside Ottawa. It is simply the cost of civil government, the overhead cost of managing the machine, and I submit to the House and the Government that it is costing too much to run the business of this country. I am not criticising the Government for a moment; I am not disposed to criticise the government that preceded this one, for I had twenty-two months' experience in a government and I know how difficult it is to keep down expenditure, but I do say in all seriousness that the time has come in this country when there should be a thorough examination and revision not only of the cost of civil government, but of administering the whole government machinery outside of the head offices at Ot-CMr. Crsrar.l
*tawa, to see wherein economies may be effected. ' We cannot tax the people of Canada at the rate of $450,000,000 or $500,000,000 a year, and expect the country to prosper, and if I may offer this suggestion, I think the Government would be well advised-and in this I am confident that they would have the whole-hearted support of the Canadian people-to set about seriously to consider where the cost of running the machinery may be cut down not only in the city of Ottawa but throughout the whole Dominion.

Perhaps in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette, and in View of the minister's own declaration that he finds >his department exceedingly well run, he will now consent at least to say that extravagance shall stop or that it is not going on in his department, and will reduce this vote to the amount asked for last year. If we are to practise economy, this is the time to start.
I cannot add anything very much to what has been so ably said by the hon. member for Marquette nor indeed to the very frank admission of the minister himself, that he finds his department well run. Surely in this year of contraction and further deflation, there ought not to be an increase in the cost of administration, but rather economy, and I would suggest that the minister seriously consider cutting down this vote.

The contention was not that. The contention was that the work was already being done by the Department of Interior and that there was mere duplication in the Conservation Commission. It appears, according to the minister, and I have no doubt he is right, that eight clerks were tansferred from the Conservation Commission to the Interior Department, but those should have taken the place of men who dropped out by death, superannuation or resignation. It is that, the minister, I think, has failed to take account of.
