I was merely asking for the purpose of showing that there would be a saving, and that it would be an argument in favour of turning over the natural resources to the provinces.

The thought has occurred to me that it is possible our Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) would like to bring down a huge credit balance next year, and on that account he has not been very severe in his criticisms of his ministers when they have presented their budgets to him. The time to practise economy is right now, and surely from all the expressions that have been given on both sides, particularly the Government side, it is apparent the House has indicated its approval of the principle of economy. We are everlastingly talking economy on this side. We believe we should have economy, and yet in every case excuses or reasons are given why each particular department should be sustained in its vote, practically as high as the expenditure of last year. It seems to me the excuse of the Civil Service Commission is offered too frequently. They are charged with the responsibility, but it seems like a man trying to hide behind a woman's skirts a little bit.
If the Government appreciate the position of the taxpayers throughout the country, they will deal with the question of expenditure with determination to bring the administration back to a basis of rigid economy. While it is true that the minister has only a brief acquaintance with his department, he must have had advice; but I fear his advisers have not viewed the situation from the standpoint of the taxpayers. If all these large spending departments are coming before Parliament and asking for the same amounts of money as have been spent in recent years we must simply insist upon the Government putting into practice those principles of economy which have been enunciated on all sides. We must demonstrate by our votes that we are going to put in practice that which we preach. The ministers must accept the principle that economy has to be practised and the principle must be illustrated by the amount of money that Parliament is asked to vote.

Civil Government-Labour-salaries and contingencies, $304,255.

It will be noted that the civil government Estimates for the Department

Supply-La bour
of Labour for the fiscal year 1922-23, as prepared, show an increase of $23,400. This increase is explained as follows. Under the present regulations of the Civil Service Commission, it is necessary to provide for payment for positions resulting from promotions or changes in duties, before the positions are actually created by Council. There are in the Estimates now before the Committee a number of such positions, that is, a position specified with a stated salary opposite it, which position has not yet been created or filled, but which it is believed to be necessary to create and fill.
Would it be convenient to give a list of those at this moment?

Let us take the third specified position-Director of Technical Education. Since I have been minister of the department, we have had no Director of Technical Education. That official was taken from the Dominion Government by the Government of British Columbia, and we have not yet filled the position. I do not know just when we shall fill it, but possibly we shall not fill it for the next few months. ;It, however, appears necessary to place in the Estimates an amount to cover the salary for such an official, if it be found that we can get the proper and desirable man to fill the position, and if we think the time opportune to appoint such an official.
What are the duties of a Director of Technical Education in this department?

The Director of Technical Education has, in co-operation and conjunction with the provincial educational authorities, the duty entrusted to him of maintaining timely supervision of the expenditures of the amounts of money granted by this Government to assist provincial governments in providing for proper technical education in the various provinces. As the hon. gentleman will know, this Government has a specified vote which, this particular year, amounts to $1,100,000, and which is apportioned on a certain basis prescribed by law and on an equal basis as between the provinces, to promote and further technical educational advantages to the youth of the various provinces. Those are, as best I can describe them, the duties of the Director of Technical Education. At the present time we have an Assistant
Director of Technical Education, who is carrying on with the assistance of one or two stenographers, I am not sure just how many.	*

This, perhaps, affords an illustration of the manner in which these expenditures grow. As we well know, education is a matter entirely within the control of the provinces, and I think it should remain there. I know a good many of my hon. friends opposite agree with me in that view. It is of doubtful wisdom to develop in any branch of the federal government any staff or group of people whose business it is to mix up in the function of education which is particularly a function belonging to the provinces. If the federal authorities desire to assist and promote technical education in the various provinces, that can surely be done without the need of building up a staff of educational experts in our Labour Department. This is an item upon which we could have a little enlightenment.
I am quite sure the hon. member for Marquette will not hold me responsible for the condition that I find in this respect.
Not for a moment.

I am quite sure he will agree with me that, even though his views are absolutely correct and this House should conform thereto, it would be necessary to change an existing law. Under the existing arrangements and the law placed upon the statute book by the government which preceded us, we have a graduated, increasing amount of money provided by the federal government to assist, on a fifty-fifty basis, the various provincial governments in promoting proper technical education amongst the young people of those provinces. If the views of my hon. friend were to prevail, it would, of course, be necessary to eliminate the law now existing, which provides in the present year for a fund of $1,100,000, or $100,000 in excess of the amount provided for in last year's Estimate, and we would, in substance, be saying to the various provincial authorities: No longer will the federal government undertake to uphold the hands of the provinces or to assist them in providing technical education for their young people. I think my hon. friend will agree that to maintain the necessary and timely supervision over that federal expenditure of $1,100,000 during the present year, it is not unreasonable
Supply-Labour

that there should be a director of technical education. We have not one now, and there should be such an officer; and we should also have an / assistant director, because there might be something to do in two provinces at the same time. A couple, but not more than a couple, of stenographers are also needed, or approximately a staff of four, to maintain the supervision over the expenditure of this money during the present fiscal year.

I am aware of the legislation by which this assistance was given for technical education, but I do not think that it provides for any Director of Technical Education, or Assistant Director. That was what I was drawing my hon. friend's attention to. As regards his last statement, it is a fact, for instance, that the federal government pays large subsidies to certain provinces in Canada, but because that is done, under the law there is no provision that there should be a staff of experts to supervise, with the provincial authorities, the expenditure of those subsidies.
I regret that I have not with me a copy of the statutes. I had understood that the law specifically provided that there shall be a director.

If that is so I stand

In view of the fact that the position which the minister speaks of was marked up against last year, so that it does not x-epresent an increase, why is it that the total number of employees for the coming year is 11 more than in the preceding year? And before the minister answers this question perhaps he will answer another. He has spoken of technical education. Perhaps the House will be interested to know his view as to whether or not the Dominion Government should take part in technical education.

The last question is indeed a fair one and I personally regard it as commendable that the federal government should show a disposition to cooperate, where desired, with the various provincial governments in promoting technical education. My hon. friend (Mr. Manion) asked why the permanent employees show an increase, the respective figures being 106 permanent employees for 1921-22 as compared with 117 for 1922-23. I am glad of the opportunity to answer the question. On the 30th of December I took

charge of the Labour Department and found the following employees therein: In Ottawa, there were fifty-one permanent ladies, and twenty-five temporary; fifteen permanent returned soldiers and seven temporary; other males, twenty-eight permanent and five temporary, or a total of ninety-four permanent and thirty-seven temporary. Outside of Ottawa, at the employment offices in Calgary, Winnipeg, Vancouver and other points, there were three permanent ladies and four temporary, three permanent returned soldiers and one temporary; other males five permanent, or a total of 147 employees instead of the 106 which my hon. friend sees on the Estimates for the closing fiscal year. Yes, and perhaps the
minister will explain how it is that, in view of the fact, that there is to be a reduction of thirty or forty, he is increasing the estimate on civil government by $24,000.

Where are they?

This employment

While these Estimates are under discussion I desire to call the attention of the minister to a matter which in my opinion, and I believe in the opinion of the House, is of great public importance, namely, the critical situation in the coalmining districts of the maritime provinces, as a result of the strike-on-the-job which is now in progress in portions of Nova Scotia. I observe in the press that the hon. minister has declared himself in very strong terms to Mr. McLachlan, the secretary of the United Mine Workers of America, holding office in that province. Mr. Chairman, in reply to my hon. friend from York-Sunbury, when a boy I was taught "There is a time and place for everything."
This is the time and the place.

My hon. friend has intimated that he has learned through the press my personal views of the intended strike-on-the-job. speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put another question or two with regard to this statistician. From my previous question I understand that the employment specialist is largely a statistician. Now we have another statistician in the Department of Labour. A little further down we have Wage Investigators, who I presume are also statisticians. Then a little further down we have Principal Statistical Clerks, who I presume, are statisticians. Then we have Junior Wage Investigators, who, I assume, are also statisticians. My hon. friend evidently thought I was too slow in running down the list, so he proceeded to get ahead of me. If he will bear with me patiently I will endeavour to go over each of these positions and discuss them for his benefit. The position of statistician is not a new one, though we are going to ask the Civil Service Commission to provide definitely for the classification of this employee. The duty of the statistician relates to the comparison of prices, the particulars concerning which you will find in the Labour Gazette. He has to secure accuracy in the comparison of those prices and make a correct estimate of the cost of living from time to time. Then we come to the head clerk. The minister was good enough to read me a little lecture a moment ago as to times and places. May I ask him if any of his investigators are in Cape Breton at the present time, and if so who they are, and what progress they are making?
The answer to the first question is, No; therefore there is no necessity of answering the others.

I am very grateful for the information the minister has given me with regard to four out of eleven permanent employees outside of Ottawa who, he says, are included in this list. If he will inform me with respect to the other seven, I shall be obliged.

I must ask the hon. member for Vancouver also to hear with me. I have started to do that several times, but have been tripped before I got through. I will try to get through the whole list. Now, we are asking the House to provide for five wage investigators instead of four.
You have already given that. I am anxious to get information with regard to the others.
The minister has not finished his initial list. If my hon. friend will bear with him, I think it is only fair that he should have a chance to do so.

I started at the beginning of the list and am trying to deal specifically with each of the changes. I was going on to say that the fifth wage investigator is a gentleman in the province of Quebec whom we have been paying on the basis of $15 a day, but for whom we now ask you to provide a stated yearly salary of $1,980 in case it should be found necessary to use his services continuously.
What are the duties of these wage investigators, and what control have they over wages paid or received?

These wage investigators are skilled in the comparison of wage rates as paid to various classes of employees. As you know, for many years the Government has had a fair wage policy, and it is necessary quite frequently to investigate what the fair wages in any particular class of employment may be in a certain locality. To illustrate, recently we found it necessary to place two wage investigators in the Niagara Peninsula to ascertain comparative fair wage rates for various classes

Supply-Labour
of employees engaged on the Welland Ship Canal. As the hon. member for Vancouver will know, one of these wage investigators undertakes, under the direction of the department, to maintain supervision over comparative fair wage rates in the mining industry on Vancouver Island; and he has been entrusted by employer and employees with the duty of determining from time to time what should be the graduated scale of wages paid in the coal mining industry.
But not in Cape Breton.

Have the Fair Wage Investigators anything to do with farm labour? To make clear the purport of my question, I may say that I have had i Considerable to do with this matter in the western territory, particularly in Saskatchewan, and I know that there is a real effort being made in those provinces by the provincial departments of labour to standardize the wages of farm labourers. They have been attempting to do that for two years. I think the first attempt was made in the summer of 1920, but they did not get very far. The officials met again a year later, and made a little more progress, and I happen to know they are attempting another step in advance this year. I should like to know if these Fair Wage Investigators have anything to do with that, and if so, what progress they are making.

Do I understand my
hon. friend to suggest that the Fair Wage Investigators of the federal department of Labour have been undertaking to interfere with the wages paid to farm labourers in Western Canada?

That
was not my point. I know that the provincial departments of labour, in co-operation with the employers of labour on the Prairie provinces and with the employees, are attempting to evolve some system of standardizing the wages that will be fair both to the farmers and farm labourers. It may not seem to the committee to be a matter of importance, but there are many thousands engaged every year in seasonal occupations in Western Canada. Does the provincial department co-operate with the federal department? Have representatives of the federal department attended the conferences that have taken place, and if so, what part have they taken in them.

My hon. friend is right to the extent that the Dominion Government
bears one-half of the cost of the employment service, although permitting the provinces to maintain a large control over the manner of conducting that service. If my hon. friend has heard of any Fair Wage Investigators being connected with these matters, it is only in an advisory capacity to the provincial employment service officer, and only for the purpose of seeing that the money of the federal 'Government was spent wisely and well. Our Fair Wage Investigators have no other authority in matters of that kind.

Have the Fair Wage Investigators authority to investigate the wages paid to men in the employment of private companies or are their investigations confined to government works? If these Investigators have authority to investigate the wages paid to labourers by employers generally, how is it that they are not investigating these cases in Nova Scotia at the present time? If they are investigating those cases, what power has the government to put their recommendations into effect? I ask merely to ascertain what are the functions of these officials, and what authority they have in this matter.

No Fair Wage officer of the federal government has any right or authority to interfere in the matter of the wages paid by private concerns. His investigation in that respect resolves itself merely into ascertaining what are the wages paid for the purpose of determining what would be a fair wage on government works in the district.

What are the
duties of the Industrial Engineer?
He was at first assistant to the Director of Employment Service, and handled the work of the Department in the absence of his superior.
He is simply an assistant to the director?

He is now used for
general utility purposes in connection with employment and other questions. The next increase we come to is that of Junior Wage Investigator. Last year there was one such officer; this year we are suggesting that there should be two.

What about the
Senior Wage Investigator?

I thought I had explained that that was the position we were

proposing for the gentleman at Calgary who has supervision over the entire coal mining industry in British Columbia, off the Island, and in Alberta. He is a very capable official.
What is his name?
Mr. F. E. Harrison.

I suppose that the minister, being young in office, has not yet given much thought to economy, for I notice there are increases practically all the way through his sub-departments. I understood from his speeches in Toronto during the election campaign that he would introduce new and better methods for carrying on the work, but he seems to have surrounded himself with a small standing army of officials so that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like him and all his retinue. For example, I notice there is an Editor of Copy at $2,160. What are his duties?
I understood the hon. gentleman took the position in reference to his annual Estimates that he was introducing new methods and creating economy by just advising capital and labour to get together- he said it was a state of mind. This is the most criticized department in the public service all over Canada. Some officials are merely paper officials. I happen to have had some experience as a municipal officer for seventeen years under many governments past and present, and I say in reference to some officials here that their work is more on paper than real when you sum up the effect of it. I found the minister going to Toronto and a report was published of a speech he made at a Methodist church one Sunday night on what he was going to do-he was going to settle the labour problems probably in the same way that he lowered the high cost of living. He told his hearers that he was going to introduce new ways and means to effect economy. I am sorry I have not the article here. It relates to the first page of these Estimates. He was going to do something by compelling "capital and labour" to get together. What he meant and how he was going to do it he never said. What does he need with all these officials? He said you had to consider the state of mind of the people. Whatever he meant by that I do not know. We find now that he has publicity agents, editors, subeditors and an employment specialist. How any people has this latter officer got jobs for? We have several thou-
sand out of employment in the place I come from. Further down he has 148 officials as against 130 last year, although now there is less work. Then he has a senior wage investigator, publicity clerk, editor and junior wage investigator. I suppose they will check up the editor. Then further down he has statistical clerks, a number of them, and clerk stenographers, probably to check up the statistical clerks; junior statistical clerks to check up some other set of clerks; secretary to executive, and editor of copy. He does not say what kind of editor. Does he hand out copy for the minister? Then there are assistant editors, one at $1,800 and one at $1,440. What are their duties? Do they work eight hours a day, or like the minister 24 hours a day? Then you have a translator $1,410, then editorial assistant at $1,275. You would think you were running a newspaper office instead of a Department of Labour. As a new member of the House I do not want to criticize the minister. He has not had time to look over the department, but this is one of the most extravagant departments of the public service and one full of frills and fads. I would like to say that a little economy would not have a bad effect on the department. If he can do so well in three months wait till you see the minister's estimates next year. If he can present such estimates after he has been in office two or three months what will they be next year, with the list of editors, supervisors, and other members of his retinue? On the next page they go from $108,000 to $192,000, and further on you come to the Labour Branch confidential messengers ; two messenger clerks, probably confidential clerks to check up the other two messengers, and then contingencies, clerical and other assistants, including the minister's assistants. Then we have confidential messenger to the minister. He is not satisfied with the other messenger, but wants to have one of his own. Then you come to the printing and stationery bureau. What about the editor of copy? I think altogether too much copy has been given out by the minister and this department. His business and that of the department is to settle strikes, but I never knew them to settle strikes yet. We had several strikes in Toronto and all the department would do would be to wire or come down to the city and ask the municipal authorities to settle a strike. I think the department is overmanned. I think they

Supply

Labour
could do with less men especially in view of the explanation of the Government that they are practising- economy. Let us start in each department and let us get rid of the frills and fads with which this department is honeycombed. There are more frills in this department than any other department of the public service and I say that without fear of contradiction. I have had a good deal to do with this department. The minister went on to speak of the high cost of living. Let him investigate the price of coal. Soft coal at the Virginia mines is quoted at $1.10 a ton at the mines and hard coal at $6 a ton at the Pennsylvania and other mines. With all these officials why cannot the minister do something to get a reduction in the price of coal? What is he doing to bring down the price of coal? Is he going to bring the producer and consumer together? I am sorry to detain the House so long but I think the House is entitled to more information on each of these items.
The provinces have labour departments and the larger cities have labour and unemployment departments. Is there overlapping? We hear about the people who are out of work in Toronto and other large places. True it is, this Government has had to dole out some money, but they could have done a great deal more if they had reduced expenses by cutting down the number of these useless officials. If they will bring down the cost of civil government they will be doing something towards effecting economy. The question of economy in Estimates is before the United States Congress to-day. They are reducing estimates over there and the municipalities are struggling to reduce estimates. Yet here is the minister coming to the House with a big increase in his Estimates. Although we are told that the relations between capital and labour to-day are happy, the minister's advice is for them to get together. If this is done he should not need these various officials, because if they adopt the principle of getting together it is so much the better for labour and capital and I do not know what he will want the 148 officials for.
I would like some Progressive to go through the Labour Department and see what the officials are doing. Are they settling strikes? I do not wish to criticize them too much. They have done some good work I suppose, but I say these officials are not all necessary and that the Labour Department is often a paper organization
so far as settling strikes go. Then you have the question of the Industrial Disputes Act which does not apply to a public utility, such as water-power, electric railway and electric light companies, operated by the people-and yet you have those officials who are going about the country, spending money and advising these publicly-owned enterprises to appoint boards to settle strikes.
I think if the hon. minister would go slowly in his Estimates when he is just starting, look further into the department and cut out some of the frills and fads it would be better for the House and the country and we would get better results for the money expended and promote the true and best interests of labour.

Mr. Chairman, I am extremely gratified to know that the member from North Toronto (Mr. Church) is here to deal with these questions in his usual way, and I am particularly gratified to note that he appears to be in the same state of mind and body that I have known him tc be for many years in dealing with any such question as the one he has undertaken ta analyze during the last few minutes. I regard it as a special honour for a young minister to have had so much attention paid to him as has been bestowed on me by the hon. member for North Toronto. But in disregard of all the views expressed by my hon. friend, I will undertake to proceed with a consistent and business-like analysis of these Estimates that are being submitted to you, and to show you wherein such increases appear to be necessary on the basis of the amounts that were regarded as necessary by the present Opposition, when it was the government last year. If, as stated by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), this Labour department is a paper organization, and unnecessary, as I understood him to intimate, he might surely, for the protection of the reputation of his party, have kept that fact a secret for at least a little while longer, because I want to inform the hon. gentleman, what he was not here to receive a short time ago, namely that when I took hold of this department, there were in it 147 employees, 42 of whom were temporary and we now propose to make twelve of those temporary employees permanent, who will perform largely the same duties as they have been performing, and to discontinue, so far as possible, the services of the other temporary employees. I am sure, too, that the labouring men in Toronto, in whom my

Supply-Labour

hon. friend has expressed, in years gone by under certain conditions, such an earnest interest, will be highly edified, on reading Hansard or the papers, if they take the trouble to quote the hon. gentleman, to learn that his estimate tof the Labour department and its functions during the present and the past government, is that it is useless, of no effect and no good, a paper organization. My experience has been that the labouring men in Toronto and elsewhere have, at times held the view that sufficient consideration has not been given to the aims, claims and rights of labour, and that there should be rather a broadening than a contraction of the efforts of the Labour department. But we, tonight, have had the honour of listening to the advice of the hon. member for North Toronto, who intimates that there is nothing to that department; that it should all be wiped out. I am sure the labouring men of Toronto will be very much edified to hear of the latest stunt of the hon. member for North Toronto.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

It would
surely never do to check the minister in his statement.
Order.
I was just referring to the fact that it would never do to interrupt the minister in order to pass this resolution, and I was called to order.

We then come to the
senior statistical clerks, of whom there were six last year.
Has the minister not missed the Publicity Assistant?
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; I have.

Will the
minister be good enough to tell the com-miteee what are the duties of the publicity agent proper, before we take up the question of his assistant?

The publicity agent, I am told, draws what many hon. members may have seen at times, charts indicating the fluctuations as between supply and demand in the labour market in Canada, for the information of those who are interested in such matters. He also draws such charts and gives such publicity to the charts and to other information as would
[Mr. Murdock.3
appear advisable to assist in equalizing, so far as possible, employment throughout this Dominion.
Does he draft the political chart too?
I think not.
My hon. friend evidently lost his.

I might say to my hon. friend that, if he was drawing political charts, he would show to-morrow morning a largely rising margin as regards major-' ities. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) asked me about the publicity assistant. I am told that is just a classification which the Civil Service Commission have given to this clerk, classifying and specifying the work and defining the duties.
Is his work defined as assistant to the publicity agent proper?
I was speaking aboui the publicity agent.
I thought you were speaking about the publicity assistant?
The hon. member is right.

The reason I asked the minister the question was that I noted by the Estimates that the publicity agent is apparently a new officer this year. I thought it would be fair to inquire if the work had doubled.

The work has not
changed whatsoever; but the Civil Service Commission have defined the duties, and have classified the position as publicity assistant.
How was he classified last year?
I am told that the position was classified heretofore as a senior clerk, although the clerk was performing the duties now being performed and which it is proposed shall continue.
What is his name?

M. K. Roughsedge. The next is an additional senior statistical clerk whom we are asking shall be provided for on a permanent basis. He has been

Supply-Labour
performing the duties during the past fiscal year.
That is a promotion.

It is a promotion on the permanent classification. The next item is for 14 statistical clerks instead of 13, an addition of one, and then the increase in salary for the other clerks. Next is 14 clerk stenographers instead of 11. Two of them have been there during the entire past fiscal year on a temporary basis and on certificate; the third additional clerk is a temporary employee being promoted on a permanent basis. Then we are asking for five office appliance operators instead of four. In this instance we are again asking to have placed on a permanent basis an employee who has been carried throughout the past fiscal year as a temporary employee.
What are the duties of the office appliance operators?

Notwithstanding the length of time which the member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) credits me with having been in the Labour department-almost three months-I have not had the opportunity, which I should like to have and which I hope I shall have, to investigate fully the working of the various branches of the department. I have, however, seen some of the office appliances that are used, and I should be glad indeed if any hon. gentleman would visit the Labour department and inspect the appliances that are used for the purpose of tabulating promptly and accurately certain results that are required from time to time to indicate the unemployment condition throughout Canada as well as many other matters upon which it is desired to secure absolutely accurate and reliable figures that cannot be controverted or disputed.
Are these employees operators of tabulating machines?

Tabulating, mimeographing, multigraphing and some other larger machines. We have in particular in the department one machine which we cannot buy. I understand that we pay a rental of $100 a month for it, that being the only basis on which we can secure it. My predecessor thought that it was worth the money many times over and I have no reason to- dispute his opinion in this regard. In the next item we ask for two additional
30i
junior clerk stenographers, who we feel are needed. These two additional clerk stenographers have been employed during the past year on a temporary basis, and it would appear to be consistent to come into the open and classify them on a permanent basis if they are to continue in the department. And that is what we are asking to do. My hon. friends will agree that that covers the additional increases in the permanent staff of the Labour department. I again call attention to the fact that there are about 30 temporary employees who were there when I came to the department and who are not provided for in these civil government estimates that are being considered. I do not know whether they can all be entirely dispensed with or not, but if they can, I assure hon. members, and especially the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) that they will be.
What saving does the minister expect to make in getting rid of the thirty employees?

In regard to such of them as we find it possible or necessary, through lack of funds, to dispense with, the saving would, of course, be in their salaries, whatever they might be. Most of them would no doubt be employees with lower grade salaries.

But I understood that my hon. friend was making some real economies in connection with the Outside Service. He is now contemplating dispensing with thirty. I should like to know what salaries these thirty are getting and What saving the minister expects to effect in connection with them. I feal that the minister is perhaps holding back a little bit. He is not quite sure that he can dispense with any of them.
If my hon. friend would like to go over the entire list of forty-two temporary employees I could tell him what they are getting.
My hon. friend need not concern himself about being fair to me; the hon. member for North Toronto will look after that.

Why are there 117 officials as against 106 last year? I see that
Supply-Labour

there are planning clerks, filing clerks, and so forth. What are the duties of these various clerks?
If my hon. friend will clearly state what information he desires I shall try to give it.

If the minister will give the information it will help him in putting through his estimates. I see there are planning clerks. . What do these men do? Do they plan election campaigns? Then I see there are filing clerks. What are their duties? Do they file the minister's speeches?

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from North Toronto reminds me, in spite of myself, of the reply of the thief on the cross. I might call his attention to the fact that we have not yet got to the Estimates which he a moment ago was so interested in inquiring- about; we have only been considering so far the Estimates of the Labour department. But we were not going fast enough for the impatient criticisms of my hon. friend; he must get ahead of the wagon and take up the Printing Bureau Estimates before we come to them, starting in with some of his characteristic criticisms.

We have been treated I think with a very plain and very patient explanation by the minister, Mr. Chairman, but with all due deference to him I must insist on bringing him back to the point where I had him very successfully a while ago. He very kindly gave me the positions of four of the twelve employees I asked him about. Really there are sixteen included in this list. He has not given me the other seven permanent and five temporary employees outside of Ottawa. While referring to that I wish to make another observation. We have in his statement a reduction of thirty employees. If that reduction is real, I wish frankly to congratulate him, because it is a step in the right direction. But with a reduction of thirty employees, which, to use his own expression, he has asserted with characteristic emphasis, we find an increase in the amount asked for of a little over $23,000. I want my hon. friend to get my point, because this is really the value of his economy, if there is any economy in it at all. Thirty less employees. Very good. But surely we do not need $23,000 more to pay for the remaining 117?

I thought I went over the eleven additional positions which we

are making permanent, but which heretofore have been temporary.

Perhaps I have not made myself clear. A few minutes ago my hon. friend told me there were eleven of these employees outside of Ottawa. He explained to me four of them very satisfactorily. Now I should like to have an explanation regarding the balance, and also regarding the increased amount.
My hon. friend must have misunderstood me. We have eleven permanent employees outside of Ottawa and only five temporary employees.
Where are they employed?

One fair wages officer in Vancouver with a temporary stenographer; another fair wages officer at Calgary; another at Toronto, and a stenographer; in Montreal a fair wage investigator, a permanent employee; in Winnipeg we have a superintendent of the western provinces for the employment service, with two statistical clerks and one clerk stenographer.
Are they temporary or permanent?

The clerk stenographer is temporary. There are two temporary junior clerk stenographers. In Halifax we have a clearance officer on a permanent basis, also a clerk stenographer with him on the same basis.

That accounts for
seven permanent and five temporary employees. There are eleven permanent employees in this vote.

One of them is not on a permanent basis but on the basis of $15 a day when required, as I stated; and another is a fair wage officer transferred to the Labour department on February 4, 1921, and on a temporary basis heretofore. Does that give my hon. friend the information that he requires about the eleven?
Yes. I am sorry it has given my hon. friend so much trouble; I had no idea it would do so. Now will he explain the discrepancy in the additional amount for the reduced staff?

Under the present
regulations of the Civil Service Commission it is necessary to provide for payments in respect of positions resulting from promotions or changes in duties before the positions are actually created by Council.

Questions
But you need not create them.

If the Minister requires 148 officers to solve labour problems of the country, how many would he require to solve the high cost of living problem about which he talked so much during the election and has referred to so often since he became minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If within a little time we might pass this item it would be worth while remaining; otherwise I suggest that we adhere to our wholesome but unwritten rule of adjourning at eleven o'clock.

Hear, hear.
Progress reported.
